title: Vedanta (revisited)
hook: a father's short line to his son, "you are that", and three great teachers who hear it three ways

segments.voice: Yesterday Vedanta pointed like a branch at the moon: Brahman, that from which the world is born. What did you trace back a few steps? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.
screen: `THE BRANCH AND THE MOON.` · `ONE LINE, THREE HEARINGS.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi. You are that. A father says it to his son in the Chandogya Upanishad, again and again, after showing him salt dissolved in water and a seed split open to nothing you can see. And here is the surprise. Three of Vedanta's great teachers, Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva, each honor this line and build on it. And they don't hear it the same way. Same words, same Upanishad, same Brahma Sutra underneath. Today we sit at one table with the three of them and let each one read the line aloud.
screen: `TAT TVAM ASI.` → `ONE LINE EVERYONE HONORS.` → `THREE TEACHERS AT ONE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Shankara reads it straight. You, at your deepest, are Brahman. Not part of it, not near it. Advaita teaching offers an image: the sense of being a separate little self is like the space inside a clay pot: break the pot and nothing goes anywhere. The space was never two. His school is called Advaita, not-two. Ramanuja reads the same line and keeps the self real. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of the one who dwells within all things, whom the things don't know, whose body they are, who guides them from inside. For Ramanuja, that's the key. The world and every self are like Brahman's body. A body is truly real, truly yours, and never apart from you. So you are that, the way a body belongs wholly to the one who lives in it. His school is called Vishishtadvaita. Madhva reads the line and hears difference. For him, Brahman, whom he knows as Vishnu, and the self are always two, and the self is wholly dependent, like a reflection that's real, but only because something shines. The line, read his way, speaks of closeness and likeness, never sameness. His school is called Dvaita, two. Three readings, each one argued with care from the same texts. Hindus who follow each line keep reading, praying and living by it to this day. The darshanas, remember, are never ranked here. Neither are these.
screen: `SHANKARA: NEVER TWO.` · `RAMANUJA: THE WORLD AS GOD'S BODY.` · `MADHVA: ALWAYS TWO, ALWAYS CLOSE.` · `THREE READINGS, NONE RANKED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the line three ways. Settle, and let the words come quietly: you are that. First, hear them as Shankara might, and rest as the open space the pot never divided. A few breaths. Then hear them as Ramanuja might, and feel your body as something you belong to, held from inside. A few breaths. Then hear them as Madhva might, and notice that you didn't make yourself shine. A few breaths. You don't have to choose. If you pray, you can let the line rest in the name you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vedanta. Today, the line you are that, heard as not-two, as body and soul, and as two who stay close. Today's word.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. Today, when someone reads something differently than you do, ask them to read it aloud their way, and just listen. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Hindus in the Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita lines each study the Upanishads through their own teacher's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the line tat tvam asi is read and taught in each lineage in its own way.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja. the Upanishad says you are that, and you're sure the self is real. how do you read it?
options: the self is an illusion after all.
the self belongs to Brahman as a body to its soul.
the line must be a mistake.
fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads the world and every self as Brahman's body: real, and never apart.

original.note: Sanskrit: you are that, from the Chandogya Upanishad, read differently by each Vedanta school.

trapdoor: what you thought: tat tvam asi means one thing in Hinduism.
what it means: the great Vedanta teachers honor the same line and read it as not-two, as body and soul, or as two who stay close.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.8.7 and after, read by Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita, with Ramanuja leaning on the inner controller of Brihadaranyaka 3.7.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7–6.16 (Uddalaka to Shvetaketu: you are that; salt in water; the seed)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the inner controller, whose body all things are)
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on Chandogya 6.8.7 and on the Brahma Sutra

notes: The pot-space image (ghatakasha) is standard in Advaita teaching; confirm it fits Shankara rather than only later Advaita.
Ramanuja's body-soul reading (sharira-shariri bhava) and use of Brihadaranyaka 3.7: confirm.

Madhva's reading: the script says only that he hears closeness and likeness, never sameness, and uses the reflection image (pratibimba). Some in his line read the sandhi as 'atat tvam asi'; deliberately left out. A Dvaita Keeper should check the framing.
The salt and seed teachings in Chandogya 6 are paraphrased and ordered loosely; confirm.

Editor: replaced 'the great Vedanta teachers all honor this line' with a claim limited to the three teachers named; the pot-space image is now credited to Advaita teaching, not to Shankara directly; the carry is spoken as 'Vedanta, revisited'.
